title: Celibacy and married priests (CCC 1579–1580)
hookLine: Latin priests are usually celibate; Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men

cards: 'Father, is that your wife?' A first-time visitor asks it at coffee hour, after the Divine Liturgy at an Eastern Catholic parish, and then wishes she hadn't.
The priest just laughs: yes, and those are his three kids by the donut table. She had always assumed a Catholic priest couldn't be married.
Across town, the Roman-rite pastor would tell her he promised celibacy at his ordination, and means to keep it. Both are Catholic priests, in full communion with the pope.

teach.b: Back on day one hundred thirty-one, you heard in passing that Eastern Catholic churches have married priests. Here's how that fits. The Catechism tells it as two disciplines, side by side.
In the Latin Church, ordained ministers, except permanent deacons, are normally chosen from men of faith who live a celibate life and intend to stay celibate.

teach.h: FOR THE SAKE OF THE KINGDOM.
teach.b: Celibacy means not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God.

The Catechism calls it a sign of new life, given over to the Lord and his people with an undivided heart, and points to Jesus's saying in Matthew about those who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven.
Then it turns east. In the Eastern Churches a different discipline has long been in force.

Bishops are chosen only from celibates, but married men can be ordained deacons and priests. The Catechism calls this practice legitimate, and says these married priests bear real fruit in their communities.

Celibacy is held in great honor in the East as well, and many priests there choose it freely. East and West, a man already ordained can no longer marry. The order matters: marriage first, then ordination.
The Gospels hold both pictures. Jesus speaks of giving up marriage for the kingdom.
And Peter, the rock, had a mother-in-law: Jesus healed her of a fever in Peter's house. Two disciplines, not two priesthoods, held in one communion.
This week ran from the fruits of Communion, through conversion, penance, indulgences, anointing and Holy Orders, to today.

how: In the Latin Church, candidates for the priesthood normally promise celibacy when they are ordained; in Eastern Catholic churches, married men may be ordained deacons and priests, while bishops are chosen from among celibate clergy.

games.q: a married man in an Eastern Catholic church feels called to the priesthood. what does the Catechism allow?

games.why: in the Eastern Churches married men can be ordained deacons and priests. bishops are chosen from among celibates.

practice: A priest has a family too: parents who raised him, brothers and sisters, and for some a wife and children who share him with a whole parish.

Picture one of those families, a mother waiting for a phone call, a child whose father is called out at dinner to a hospital. If you pray, ask God to bless them; if you don't, just hold them kindly in mind.

wordCard.voice: Celibacy. Not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God: the usual discipline for Latin priests, and the rule for bishops in the East, where married men may be ordained deacons and priests. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: two traditions. One Church, one communion, honoring both of them. That's the week.
